claims.text: A new approach can predict the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Local chemical fluctuations relevant to thermal transport are induced by constituent-element electronegativity differences.
Constituent-element mass contributes to local chemical fluctuations relevant to thermal transport.
The HfNbTaTiZr initial structure may be random or ordered.
Altering alloy composition introduces or tailors local chemical fluctuations.
The prediction applies from 300 to 1200 K.
The prediction applies to an HfNbTaTiZr sample containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Local chemical fluctuation is a structural mediator of the predicted thermal-transport response.
Dislocation nucleation and mobility mediate the predicted thermal-transport response.
Local chemical fluctuations scatter heat-carrying phonons.
Phonon scattering caused by local chemical fluctuations reduces lattice thermal conductivity.
Accounting for local chemical fluctuations will improve prediction of HfNbTaTiZr lattice thermal conductivity over previous analytical approaches.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be comparable to experimental values of 10–17 W/(K m).
Previous analytical approaches do not account for local chemical fluctuations.
The approach is applicable from 200 to 1500 K.
The approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr with varying oxygen content.
The relationship between local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity remains incompletely understood.
Interactions between lattice and electronic heat transport may affect the prediction.
Nanoindentation and molecular-dynamics simulations can be used as experimental techniques to measure lattice thermal conductivity, dislocation behavior, and local chemical fluctuation.
A discrepancy greater than 10% between predicted and experimental lattice thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated condition limits applicability to 300–1200 K, whereas the boundary expands it to 200–1500 K without explaining the different limits.
The conditions specify a sample with exactly 1 wt.% oxygen, while the boundary claims applicability to varying oxygen contents.

The hypothesis targets lattice thermal conductivity, but the 10–17 W/(K m) comparison is presented without separating lattice and electronic contributions; this conflicts with the acknowledged possibility of interactions between those channels.
Dislocation nucleation and mobility are listed as mediators, but the mechanism only connects local chemical fluctuations to phonon scattering and gives no role for dislocations.
